meta.title: Bulgarian A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Bulgarian → English (see the Bulgarian, recall the meaning) and English → Bulgarian (see an English meaning, recall the Bulgarian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded Bulgarian word list is published that a deck could take whole, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 388 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, people and family, numbers, telling the time, days, months and seasons, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, everyday verbs, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and conjunctions every sentence is built out of — and the other 112 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Bulgarian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in Cyrillic with its stress marked (кни́га, чета́), because Bulgarian stress can fall on any syllable and move as the word changes (град, градове́), and nothing else shows it; there is no transliteration, and the Bulgarian Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters. A verb is given in its first person singular present, the form a Bulgarian dictionary lists (чета́ 'I read', glossed 'to read'), since Bulgarian has no infinitive. The 195 nouns show their gender, their definite form (Bulgarian puts 'the' on the end of the word: кни́гата), their plural and, where it differs, the form used after a number; the 102 verbs show their aspect, imperfective or perfective, with the other verb of the pair beside them, their ти form and their past; and behind the All forms fold every noun's forms and every verb's present, past tenses and imperative by person, with the personal pronouns' full and short forms. Real example sentences come with 488 of the 500 words, three apiece for 471 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, aspect, stress and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

fields.English:
particle
  1. word used to indicate agreement or acceptance: yes
  2. used to express a command
  3. used to express a wish
conjunction
  1. particle: used to mark an infinitive, to (or in some other cases, such as with modal verbs, it is not translated)
  2. if (only for conditions that are known to be false)
fields.Examples:
Дай да го видя.
Let me see it.
Да ти е сладко!
Enjoy your meal!
Не можах да спя.
I couldn't get to sleep.

fields.English:

  2. accusative reciprocal pronoun, denoting that the agents perform the mutual actions among themselves; corresponds to each other, one another
  3. reflexive pronoun, part of autocausative verbs, denoting that the referent represented by the subject combines the activity of actor and undergoes a change of state like a patient
fields.Examples:
Ти ли се обади?
Did you call?
Пази се от мен.
Keep away from me.
Пази се от Том.

  2. dative reciprocal pronoun, denoting that the agents perform the mutual actions among themselves; corresponds to (to/for) each other, (to/for) one another

fields.Examples:
